_note: Curated pool from the Dickson Baseball Dictionary via baseball-almanac.com. Faithful condensations for daily use; each entry links its source.

terms.def: An easily caught, high lazy fly ball that lets a fielder camp under it.
terms.origin: May trace to grocery clerks tipping canned goods off high shelves with a pole to catch them.

terms.def: A ball chopped down near the plate that bounces so high the batter can beat it out for a hit.
terms.origin: Named for the 1890s Baltimore Orioles, whose hard-baked infield made the bounce a weapon.

terms.def: A cheap hit that loops just over the infielders but drops in front of the outfielders.
terms.origin: H.L. Mencken called it 'a pop fly which nevertheless takes the batter to first base.'

terms.def: A left-handed pitcher or thrower.
terms.origin: By 1889 it had settled specifically onto lefty pitchers.

terms.def: A noisy on-field argument or ruckus with the umpires.
terms.origin: Broadcaster Red Barber popularized it in the late 1930s and '40s.

terms.def: The area where relief pitchers warm up during a game — and, by extension, a team's whole relief staff.
A team's best pitcher, usually a starter and the rock of the rotation. (Earliest sense: a run or score in 1840s baseball.)
terms.origin: Tradition credits pitcher Asa 'Acey' Brainard, who won 56 of 57 games for the 1869 Red Stockings.

terms.def: A home run.
terms.origin: Probably from 'humdinger' — something of remarkable excellence.

terms.def: A home run.
terms.origin: May have started in the Negro leagues as 'potato'; George Scott popularized 'taters' with the 1966 Red Sox.

terms.def: A pop fly that drops suddenly, like a bird shot on the wing, often falling between fielders for a hit.
terms.origin: Sportswriter usage for a blooper; syn. quail, dying swan.

terms.def: A hard-hit line drive on a rigid, low, straight path that seems to defy gravity.
terms.origin: 'You could hang a week's wash on it,' per broadcaster Red Rush; syn. rope, clothesline.

terms.def: A pitch destined to be hit for a home run — one that will 'go for' extra bases.
terms.origin: From 'go fer' (go for two, three...); Lefty Gomez is credited by some with coining it.

terms.def: Third base.
terms.origin: Coined by writer Ren Mulford after Reds 3B Hick Carpenter fielded seven sharp drives that 'almost tore him apart.'

terms.def: A home run, especially one hit a very long distance.
terms.origin: Popularized alongside the era's space program; early use described Harmon Killebrew's blasts.

terms.def: A fast, close-range pregame drill where a batter taps quick grounders to a cluster of fielders who fire the ball right back.
terms.origin: From 'pep' — the peppy, rapid-fire nature of the drill.

terms.def: A softly hit single that sneaks through the infield as if the ball had eyes.
terms.origin: Syn. ball with eyes on it.

terms.def: A running catch made at the fielder's shoe tops, just before the ball hits the ground.
A double play.
The part of the strike zone where a batter swings with the most power; hang a pitch there and invite a home run.
terms.origin: From batters 'wheeling' at the ball; also the nautical pilothouse from which a ship is steered.

terms.def: A brief trial in the major leagues by a minor-league player — figuratively, just long enough to drink a cup of coffee.
A curveball, especially a big sweeping one.
terms.origin: The two words may onomatopoetically suggest a curve; see also Lord Charles, Sir Charles.

terms.def: A fastball. 'High cheese' is one up and in.
terms.origin: From old slang where 'cheese' meant the best thing of its kind; also gives us 'the big cheese.'

terms.def: A brushback pitch thrown so high and inside the batter can supposedly hear it buzz past his jaw.
terms.origin: Older slang for idle chatter, dating to the 1820s.

terms.def: A spectacular catch — a jump, dive, flip, or roll — suggesting a circus acrobat.
terms.origin: Cubs OF 'Circus Solly' Hofman was named for his acrobatic grabs; syn. showboat catch.

terms.def: Last place — the position held by the team with the worst record.
terms.origin: Syn. basement, pit.

terms.def: The relief pitcher used to get the final outs and protect a late lead.
terms.origin: Cubs manager Herman Franks invented the modern role using Bruce Sutter only with an 8th/9th-inning lead.

terms.def: Any inning total greater than one — so called for the curves in the numerals 2 through 9.
terms.origin: A 1-0 game is one in which neither team posted a crooked number.

terms.def: Baserunners waiting to be driven home.
terms.origin: Brought to baseball by Senators broadcaster Arch McDonald.

terms.def: The dubious mark for striking out four times in a single game.
terms.origin: Three K's is a hat trick; four earns a 'sombrero' (bigger than a hat); five is the 'platinum sombrero.'

terms.def: The .200 batting-average threshold separating adequate hitters from the rest.
terms.origin: Named for shortstop Mario Mendoza (career .215); popularized by George Brett.

terms.def: An easy-to-hit pitch served right down the middle.
terms.origin: A refashioning of 'meet the ball'; syn. meat.

terms.def: A half-inning in which a pitcher strikes out all three batters on exactly nine pitches.
terms.origin: There were none from 1929–52 — but seven in 2022 alone.

terms.def: The dirt or cinder strip inside the outfield wall that warns a fielder, by feel underfoot, that the wall is near.
terms.origin: Conceived after Pete Reiser was badly hurt crashing into Ebbets Field's wall in 1947.

terms.def: A ball hit so hard and low it skids across the ground without bouncing.
terms.origin: Syn. worm killer.

terms.def: A rundown — a baserunner trapped between two bases with fielders closing in. (Also, as a verb, to hit a ball very hard.)
terms.origin: Short for 'in a pickle.'

terms.def: A ballpark whose small dimensions make home runs easy — John Updike's 'lyric little green bandbox' was Fenway.
terms.origin: After the small-town bandstands common at the turn of the century; syn. crackerbox.

terms.def: A pitcher who throws with an underhand, submarine-style delivery.
terms.origin: Syn. subway slinger; Carl Mays was the most infamous.

terms.def: The pitch thrown on a full count (3-2) — barring a foul, it decides the at-bat.
terms.origin: Syn. decision pitch.

terms.def: A late-breaking pitch thrown off a ball loaded with saliva, banned in 1920 for hygiene and to boost offense.
terms.origin: Grandfathered pitchers could keep throwing it; the last legal one was Burleigh Grimes, retired 1934.

terms.def: A slow pitch thrown with almost no spin so it flutters, darts, and dips unpredictably — sometimes moving 11 inches.
terms.origin: Perfected by Hoyt Wilhelm, Phil Niekro, and Charlie Hough.

terms.def: A pitch that breaks the opposite way from a curveball, thrown with an inward twist of the wrist. (Also: a zany player.)
terms.origin: Made famous by Christy Mathewson's 'fadeaway' and later Carl Hubbell.
